rationale: A wins because it does the adult PR work: it turns the same facts into cleaner desks, cleaner exclusions, and proof questions that would survive a reporter's first follow-up. Its angle "Duolingo's new split: chess for free, AI conversation for paying subscribers" finds a real monetization story in the facts, while B's "A profitable, public Duolingo posts a record 40% jump in daily active users" is mostly a company-performance blurb looking for an earnings peg. B has bones, but A knows which angles to kill before they embarrass the founder.
gaps_in_A: "the first public engagement figure for it" is not in the supplied facts; useful if true, but unsupported as written.
"compute-heavy video feature" smuggles in cost structure before Duolingo has supplied any cost data. A asks for proof later, but the claim is already doing work in the angle.
"free beginner chess course" invents course level. The update says a chess course launches free for all users, not that it is beginner-focused.
gaps_in_B: "The video feature is in beta now" conflicts with the supplied launch facts. The update gives beta engagement history and says paid Max subscribers can have the calls now.
"Duolingo is doubling down" is blacklisted slop and overstates intent. The facts say Duolingo is adding features, not responding strategically to critics.
"a gamified chess course" invents a feature attribute. The update says chess course, not gamified chess course.
"what that says about AI tutors that actually engage" overclaims from session length. Nine minutes shows use, not tutoring quality or learning impact.
